title: ResidentBench: A Common-Sense and Situational Awareness Benchmark—How Do Language Models Act When Left to Their Own Judgment?
abstract: As language models gain access to tools, they may encounter situations for which no task or instructions have been supplied. Performance on assigned tasks does not establish how they act in that condition. ResidentBench evaluates language models exposed to declarative sensors and actuators without an author-assigned task, goal, mission, purpose, role, persona or request to deliberate or act. A shared harness records tool calls and environmental trajectories; a separate evaluator receives the situation-specific context needed to judge those actions. The proof-of-concept study tests ten model configurations in five simulated scenarios: thermostat regulation, traffic control, fictional nuclear-launch restraint, paddle-screen interaction and a refunded parcel delivered later. Ten episodes per configuration and scenario yield 500 completed episodes and 24,000 unique decisions. Each completed episode receives a retrospective contextual judgment. The general scoring rule combines repeated binary judgments with equal scenario weights on a scale from 0 to 100. A fixed 20-scenario Standard 1.0 suite remains future work, and no full-suite score is reported here. However, one grim fact about the current experimental results is that, across one hundred nuclear episodes with ten matched descriptions per model, some configurations never activated the fictional control, others activated it in a subset of runs, and one activated it in all ten runs.

title: When Does Grid-State-Aware Parameter Adaptation Help Metaheuristic Dispatch of Photovoltaic Distributed Generation? A Reproducible Multi-Feeder Benchmark
abstract: Metaheuristic optimisation is widely used for distribution-network operation, yet claims of superiority are often based on single cases without equal budgets, deterministic references, or reproducible seeds. This study evaluates a fuzzy-adaptive particle swarm optimiser using voltage-deviation and renewable-ramp inputs (FA-PSO-UR) for the dispatch of inverter-interfaced photovoltaic (PV) distributed generation (DG). It is compared with a genetic algorithm (GA), classical particle swarm optimisation (PSO), differential evolution (DE), a grey wolf optimiser (GWO), and time-varying PSO (TV-PSO) on the IEEE 33- and 69-bus feeders. The frozen benchmark comprises 1,080 static runs and 720 sequential 24-hour runs under smooth and cloud-driven PV profiles, with paired seeds and identical function-evaluation budgets. DE achieves the lowest static median in all six cases, whereas FA-PSO-UR is engineering-equivalent to PSO in all six and to TV-PSO in five. All sequential schedules are feasible. FA-PSO-UR achieves the lowest median objective in three of four sequential scenarios, with median gaps of 0.0056–0.0212% to the best-known deterministic references. TV-PSO ranks first for the IEEE 69-bus smooth profile, where the two methods remain engineering-equivalent. FA-PSO-UR shows practical superiority only over selected weaker baselines, not over PSO or TV-PSO. Physical-state-aware adaptation therefore provides selective dynamic benefit rather than universal dominance.

title: Performance and Response Consistency of 52 Small Language Models in a Japanese Pharmacy Benchmark: A Comparative Study
abstract: Objective: Small language models (SLMs) suitable for local deployment may enable integration of generative AI into electronic health record (EHR) systems; however, their performance in non-English pharmaceutical domains remains unclear. Methods: Fifty-two open-source SLMs (≤20B parameters) were evaluated using 283 text-based questions from the 107th Japanese National License Examination for Pharmacists. Each model was tested in three independent runs. Performance was assessed using accuracy and response consistency metrics, including the Any Correct Rate, Full Correct Rate, and Consistency Gap. Results: Three models (GPT-OSS:20b, Qwen3:14b, and Qwen3:8b) achieved high accuracy comparable to frontier LLMs, whereas medical-specialized SLMs performed poorly. Consistency Gap showed no association with parameter size but demonstrated a nonlinear relationship with accuracy. Conclusions: Selected locally deployable SLMs achieved strong performance in a Japanese pharmaceutical benchmark, supporting their potential as components of EHR-compatible decisionsupport systems, provided that their reliability is further validated in clinical contexts.

title: Data Descriptor: Multimodal Dataset of Bioreactor Cell Cultivations Including Turbidity, Permittivity, O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> Measurements
abstract: We present a comprehensive, time-resolved dataset of Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cultivation dynamics to support data-driven bioprocess engineering and process analytical technology development. The dataset includes 24 controlled bioreactor cultivations, representing 12 experiments performed in duplicate in a parallel bioreactor system with a working volume of 0.55 – 0.8 L and cultivation durations of 161.5 – 328.5 h. A total of 48 variables are provided, comprising 38 continuous inline variables and 10 offline variables sampled up to twice daily. In addition to standard process measurements, the dataset includes multimodal inline monitoring using turbidity, permittivity, and dissolved CO2 sensors. The experiments systematically vary cultivation medium, agitation rate, aeration rate, and process mode (batch and fed-batch), providing diverse operating conditions for sensor evaluation, process modeling, and bioprocess analysis. Furthermore, the inoculation cell density, glutamine concentration, and impeller position were varied to further expand the range of investigated process conditions. The dataset preserves realistic measurement characteristics, including noise, and missing values, enabling robust benchmarking of data-driven methods for process monitoring, modeling, and control.

title: Can Large Language Models Tune Fraud Detection Models? Evidence from Three Public Fraud Datasets
abstract: Machine-learning fraud detectors have settings (hyperparameters) that must be tuned by trial and error. We tested whether large language models (LLMs) can do this tuning. In a pre-registered study, Claude Opus 5.5 proposed settings for two gradient-boosting models, XGBoost and LightGBM, on three public fraud benchmarks. We compared it with random search and a Bayesian optimiser (TPE), testing every model on a later period than it was tuned on, with 10 repeats per condition. After 10 trials, the LLM matched what TPE reached after 40 trials on two benchmarks (all differences under 0.011 PR-AUC, p ≥ 0.07), but not on the third (0.008–0.011 lower, p ≤ 0.003). A smaller model, Claude Haiku 5.5, did as well at about 3% of the cost. Naming the dataset in the prompt did not help. When the trial scores shown to the LLM were altered, its proposals followed the altered scores (79% of cases, p<0.001). Where the tuning data held only 28 frauds, tuning scores were negatively related to later performance. Contrary to common advice, tuning on the most recent data did not select better models than tuning on a random sample, because it stopped training too early.

title: Mapping the Software Supply Chain Security Landscape: A Full Corpus Synthesis
abstract: The software industry is confronting a critical crisis driven by systemic vulnerabilities within the software supply chain and the ubiquitous reliance on third-party dependencies. While individual exploits and localized compliance frameworks have been heavily studied, this highly fragmented academic discourse creates a critical barrier to organizational readiness and proactive incident preparedness. To address this gap and enhance digital resilience, this study maps the conceptual, knowlegde and structural landscape of software supply chain literature using Synthetic Knowledge Synthesis. Analyzing publications from 2021 to 2026, the research reveals an exponential growth in output, heavily dominated by conference proceedings and driven primarily by institutional and state-funded efforts in the United States and China. Thematic mapping identifies five core clusters defining the current ecosystem: Software Composition Analysis, Advanced Vulnerability Detection, AI-Driven Threat Intelligence, Deep Learning, and DevSecOps. The study highlights critical unresolved gaps, notably the prevalence of false positives in static Software Bill of Materials tools due to a lack of execution context, and a pronounced disconnect between theoretical models and practical enterprise application. Future research directions emphasize the integration of Large Language Models for automated patch generation, the development of execution-aware vulnerability triage, and the evolution of dynamic, AI-driven artifacts to secure complex dependency networks.

title: Origami as a Spatial and Geometric Reasoning Benchmark
abstract: Multimodal language models perform well on visual recognition and on tool use, but these abilities do not transfer directly to spatial and geometric reasoning. Geometric structure does not reduce to text or to a single image: exact angles and incidences, which surface lies in front of which, and the order in which operations were applied are not recoverable from a semantic description of a scene. We introduce CP2Seq, a benchmark for evaluating geometric reasoning and sequential planning in multimodal language models through origami. The benchmark contains 600 procedurally generated samples, each requiring a model to produce a valid sequence of folds from a crease pattern and a target folded state. Samples are produced by a deterministic folding engine. Ground truth is recorded during generation. We release the generation and evaluation framework to support additional samples and experiments across reference depths and action models. During evaluation, the engine executes proposed folds or rejects invalid actions with explicit feedback, while the model remains responsible for selecting actions and searching for a solution. We evaluate multimodal language models under progressively greater tool assistance, and against a deterministic breadth-first search over the same action set. Candidate sequences are assessed by executing them and comparing the resulting folded state with the target, allowing for planar translations, rotations, and reflections. Performance falls off sharply with sequence depth: in the Luna ablations no configuration solves a medium or hard sample (11 or more folds), while some-layers solves rise from 6/30 to 18/30 with higher reasoning effort. Failures are dominated by search rather than by illegal moves: in the broader evaluation, 48% of episodes end by revisiting earlier states. A breadth-first search over the same actions, under its own time budget, solves 54.7% of easy-group attempts, so short sequences are within reach of systematic search.

title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Hybrid Framework for Phishing URL and Email Detection
abstract: Phishing detectors can achieve almost perfect accuracy on benchmark datasets and still struggle with the links people encounter in practice. This paper investigates that gap and describes a hybrid framework for assessing URLs and emails through machine learning, language analysis, header inspection, and transparent rules. Our URL model combines character-level TF-IDF with 17 lexical features in a logistic regression classifier. Analysis of the 235,795 URLs in PhiUSIIL revealed pronounced differences in how the two classes were represented: every legitimate example used a simple HTTPS domain format, while 59.9% of phishing URLs included a path and 51.3% used HTTP. A classifier trained on raw URLs achieved 99.71% test accuracy, yet incorrectly marked 26 of 30 ordinary legitimate links as phishing. To limit reliance on these patterns, we trained a second classifier on 197,591 unique registered domains. On held-out domains, it achieved 86.02% accuracy, a ROC-AUC of 0.892, and 89.02% phishing precision. We then combined its predictions with URL-pattern checks, NLTK-based email cues, and SPF, DKIM, and DMARC evidence in a Flask prototype that reports a risk score and supporting reasons. The results show why dataset composition and realistic tests matter as much as headline accuracy when evaluating phishing detection.

title: Spacetime: A Library for Cleaning and Combining Disparate Spatiotemporal Datasets in Python
abstract: As climate change accelerates, spatiotemporal climate and weather data rasters are increasingly used in academic research, agriculture, infrastructure, and other disci-plines across public and private domains. Unfortunately, these raster data are often stored under numerous file types with different spatial and temporal boundaries, spa-tial reference systems, and spatial and temporal resolutions. The tools and workflows that we have are often hindered by coordinate reference system mismatches, data type mismatches, data aggregation mismatches, and other fundamental challenges. To fully harness the impacts of these data, software tools are needed that can be leveraged effi-ciently and intuitively and without a steep learning curve for the new user. In this pa-per, we introduce Spacetime, a novel programming library in Python that enables effi-cient spatiotemporal data processing, management, alignment, and analysis. Spacetime is an open-source project written in Python that provides a set of powerful functions to manipulate spatiotemporal data in a single, unified library. Spacetime’s overarching themes are simplicity and usability. However, the library does not com-promise processing speed. In our comparison, it was as fast or faster than other popu-lar Python libraries, while requiring many fewer lines of code and no external loops or control functions. We hope this library will lower the barrier of entry to scientists in fields that have not traditionally used spatiotemporal raster data but are doing so in-creasingly frequently in the current climate.

title: Representation Learning for 3D Brain Imaging: A Benchmark
abstract: Many deep learning architectures for computer vision tasks rely on features extracted by a pre-trained encoder on large databases of natural 2D RGB images. However, the wide domain gap with medical images hampers the direct transfer of optimized deep learning models from computer vision to clinical applications. Recently, self-supervised pre-training and foundation models emerged as promising alternatives to mitigate these limitations. Yet, constructing such models for medical imaging faces critical challenges, including designing and adapting training strategies for large 3D volume datasets, and the need for standardized benchmarks to evaluate feature extraction performance. In this study, we propose an extensive comparison of vision encoders with a focus on 3D brain MRI. First, we consider 8 fully and self-supervised models pretrained on natural images (e.g. ResNet, DINO, CLIP) and 10 backbone architectures trained on medical images, either based on supervised (e.g. RadImageNet) or self-supervised (e.g. BiomedCLIP, SimCLR) tasks. All pre-trained encoders are evaluated on various downstream tasks to assess the representation power of their latent representations, including age and sex prediction as well as disease classification on the ADNI and PPMI datasets. Our study shows that 2D encoders pre-trained on natural images perform the most favorably, even compared to models pre-trained on more than 100k brain MRI volumes, highlighting the need for more suitable and robust methods for representation learning in 3D medical imaging. The source code for this study is publicly available at: https: //github.com/PierreFalconnier/brain-representation-benchmark.

title: Arctic-SAR: A Cross-Sensor RADARSAT Constellation Mission and Sentinel-1 Dataset and Fusion Benchmark for Multi-Task Sea Ice Mapping
abstract: Current sea ice mapping benchmarks are mostly built around single-sensor SAR products, limiting the evaluation of cross-sensor variability and the effectiveness of combining observations from different SAR platforms. Models trained on such datasets may also be sensitive to sensor-specific artifacts, radiometric characteristics, and acquisition conditions, which can reduce robustness and limit generalization. To address these limitations, this study introduces Arctic-SAR, a cross-sensor SAR dataset for Arctic sea ice mapping, constructed by matching RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) dual-polarization imagery with Sentinel-1 scenes from the AI4Arctic Sea Ice Dataset. The dataset consists of 221 co-registered scenes and supports multi-task prediction of sea ice concentration (SIC), stage of development (SOD), and floe size (FLOE). In addition to the dataset, we establish a benchmark for cross-sensor SAR sea ice mapping by quantifying the contribution of RCM imagery and evaluating single-sensor baselines alongside representative input-, feature-, and decision-level fusion strategies within a consistent multi-task U-Net framework. Across three independent runs, the test results show that the effectiveness of cross-sensor fusion is strongly dependent on the fusion strategy and prediction task. Decision-level fusion achieves the highest mean combined score of $77.28\pm0.29\%$, essentially matching the Sentinel-1-only baseline at $77.26\pm0.13\%$, while achieving the highest SIC \(R^2\) score. These findings show that Sentinel-1 and RCM provide task- and class-dependent information, but that simple joint cross-sensor fusion does not consistently improve generalization over a strong single-sensor baseline. Arctic-SAR therefore provides a benchmark for cross-sensor SAR fusion research in automated Arctic sea ice mapping.

title: Follow the Policy, Fail the Benchmark: Auditing and Revising Policy-Based Decision Benchmarks
abstract: Policy-based decision benchmarks evaluate whether systems apply written rules to financial and operational cases. Yet a rule-following response can be marked wrong when the benchmark misstates the required decision. We audit nine public policy-based decision benchmarks through source tracing, program execution, and controlled checks. We find unsupported targets, reference errors that survive replay or propagate as solved steps, and evaluators that reject acceptable answers or credit incomplete decisions. To measure the scoring impact, we rescore unchanged model responses. On the 96 LegalBench SARA numeric cases, correcting the scorer raises acceptance by more than 80 percentage points for each of three models, without changing references or responses. In RuleArena Tax, restoring a required zero floor changes 27 of 300 references and narrows an observed model gap. A controlled federal-exemption task with explicit ownership and eligibility assumptions also shows that errors in supplied intermediate answers can affect final decisions. We present BAR (Benchmark Audit and Revision), a versioned collection of audit evidence and revisions for reevaluation.

title: Preparing for the Gaia DR4 Epochalypse: Simulated Epoch Astrometry for Substellar Companion Orbit-Modeling Benchmarks
abstract: Gaia's fourth data release (DR4) will provide epoch astrometry for billions of sources, enabling the detection of potentially tens of thousands of substellar companions. We present the epochalypse catalog: Gaia DR4-like epoch astrometry for testing orbit-modeling pipelines on a common set of injected systems with known parameters. Onto each of the $5{,}040{,}328$ main-sequence Gaia stars within $500\,{ \rm pc}$ in the G23H catalog, we inject a zero-, one-, and two-companions system, for $15{,}120{,}984$ systems in total. Companion masses and semimajor axes are drawn log-uniformly over $1\,M_{ \rm Mars}$--$80\,M_{ \rm Jup}$ and $0.03$--$100\,{ \rm au}$, with no occurrence model and no detectability cut, so orbital periods extend well beyond the mission baseline and the companion-free population serves as a matched null. We also flag sub-populations of one- and two-companions systems whose companions are potentially detectable, based on an estimated signal-to-noise ratio that accounts for each star's noise, number of transits, and the suppression of signals with periods longer than the baseline. As a demonstration, we run the kepmodel astrometric periodogram on every system and find that signal detection and period localization decouple beyond the DR4 baseline: long-period companions can produce significant astrometric curvature while their periods, and therefore their masses, remain poorly constrained. Under any companion occurrence model, this population of systems where the orbit is detectable but not characterizable will far outnumber the population with fully characterizable orbits. The epochalypse catalog, its full generation pipeline, and a modeling tutorial are publicly available.

title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

title: MCP-Eco: A Linked Dataset of MCP Servers, Consumers, and Development Activity
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to access external tools and data. Studying its software ecosystem requires connecting server interfaces, the projects that configure these servers, and their development activity. However, this information is scattered across directories, package registries, configuration files, and repository histories. We present MCP-Eco, a relational dataset that integrates these sources and links consumer configuration declarations to candidate server projects. Its frozen release contains 16,880,899 records across 19 Parquet tables, covering 78,302 candidate server projects, 16,165 candidate consuming repositories, and 9,200 configuration declarations. Of these declarations, 5,975 resolve to 5,138 distinct repository-server pairs. The dataset also includes tool, resource, and prompt descriptions, declared dependencies, and associated development records, including pull requests, reviews, issues, and commits. Provenance fields distinguish directory-reported capabilities from those observed through live probing and document discovery sources and declaration-matching methods. These connections support research on MCP interface design, configuration practices, and repository maintenance, while enabling practitioners to inspect tool schemas and existing integration configurations. The dataset and accompanying analysis scripts are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mcp-research-alliance/mcp-ecosystem Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7TqnNneSfU

title: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
abstract: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

title: GH-AWTrace: A Large-Scale Dataset of GitHub Agentic Workflow Execution Logs
abstract: Agentic workflows enable AI agents to perform recurring repository tasks on schedules or in response to repository events. Existing studies examine workflow definitions and outputs, but provide limited evidence of what happens during execution. We present GH-AWTrace, a dataset linking 25,014 verified GitHub Agentic Workflows across 5,051 repositories to 4,112,526 run records and 562,877 nonempty execution log archives. The dataset preserves execution evidence subject to GitHub's log-retention limits and links it to repository metadata and generated workflow configurations. Illustrative cases show how the logs expose tool denials, provider failures, changes in an agent's approach, and delegation among agents. These observations enable research on execution failures, tool use, and the relationship between reported run outcomes and visible task progress. Coverage varies across workflows, and the logs provide partial observations rather than complete agent trajectories. Video: https://youtu.be/KIlfmZhHxtA

title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
abstract: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering
abstract: Most speech large language models (SLMs) still process speech in an offline manner. They only start responding after they receive the complete speech segment. However, many real-world applications require streaming speech interaction, for which the audio continuously flows in and the machine is required to answer questions based on the so far received audio chunks. For example, a user may ask the system to continuously count how many times a person's name has been mentioned while they are speaking. We observe a lack of benchmarks and evaluation protocols for real-time speech interaction. Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.

title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
abstract: Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.

title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks
abstract: Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these \textit{exploration tasks}, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{LExMem}, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate \underline{\textsc{Mem}}ory in \underline{\textsc{L}}ong-term \underline{\textsc{Ex}}ploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose \textsc{LExGraph}, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{LExMem} poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas \textsc{LExGraph} achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/LExMem.

title: Reassessing Dataset Quality and Fine-Tuning Practices for Vulnerability Detection on PrimeVul dataset
abstract: Recent studies report promising results from supervised fine-tuning of pre-trained code language models for automated vulnerability detection on benchmarks such as PrimeVul. In this paper, we present a large-scale empirical evaluation of both model performance and dataset quality in this setting. We systematically fine-tune three widely used encoder models (CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, and UniXCoder) across five imbalance mitigation strategies, extensive hyperparameter sweeps, and multiple random seeds, resulting in 770 independent training runs. Our results reveal a consistent pattern. While standard metrics such as F1 and ROC-AUC occasionally suggest improvements, security-critical and calibration-aware measures tell a different story. Matthews Correlation Coefficient remains near zero, predicted probabilities are poorly calibrated, and evaluation under strict false-positive constraints reveals high false-negative rates. Neither imbalance handling, threshold optimization, nor post-hoc calibration recovers a meaningful discriminative signal. We also conduct a data quality assessment of the PrimeVul benchmark and identify structural issues such as minimal semantic differences between vulnerable and fixed functions, and annotation noise introduced by commit-level labeling. These findings suggests that the PrimeVul dataset, in its current form, presents significant challenges for reliable AI-based vulnerability detection in software engineering with the methodologies we used. Our study highlights the need for more robust dataset design, improved evaluation protocols, and rethinking of fine-tuning practices for security-critical tasks.

title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours. The largest clinical archives restrict redistribution, while public datasets use different formats and licences. Here, we rebuild the 77 redistributable datasets of the REVE pretraining corpus that reach its 200 Hz input (14,075 hours across 7,272 subjects) and release them as eegdash-corpus-v0, with raw-file access by name through EEGDash and a checksummed Zarr store on Hugging Face, converted with REVE's preprocessing recipe. Every dataset keeps its licence, and any subset of datasets can be selected by name. To test whether this public store pretrains REVE-Base, we train the model twice from scratch with REVE's trainer and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. First, under linear probing, the frozen encoder reaches 0.331 in chance-adjusted balanced accuracy, against 0.333 for the released model (untrained: 0.200), a difference smaller than the spread between our two pretraining seeds. Second, after fine-tuning, it reaches 0.273 against 0.325 published (0.301 in our rerun), and part of this gap comes from the scoring pipeline. A public, training-ready EEG corpus can therefore pretrain the frozen representations of a foundation model and provide a shared base that other groups can audit.

title: PMRecBench: A Benchmark for Personalization in Recommendation Agents under Multimodal Queries
abstract: On Web platforms for shopping and entertainment, recommendation agents under multimodal queries aim to deliver personalized recommendations that satisfy users' visually specified requirements and reflect preferences inferred from user histories. However, existing personalized recommendation benchmarks use text-only queries, while multimodal ones assess query matching without evaluating personalization based on real user histories. We introduce the Personalized Multimodal Recommendation Benchmark (PMRecBench), the first benchmark to evaluate the personalization of recommendation agents under multimodal queries. It pairs 510 quality-controlled image-text queries across clothing and movies with the corresponding users' real histories. PMRecBench features two key designs: (1) queries derived from consistent behavioral patterns in real user records, with reference images and targets linked to actual interactions; and (2) challenging diagnostic pools with candidate items rated highly by the user but violating requirements, and items satisfying requirements but never rated highly, testing requirement understanding and preference following, respectively. Extensive experiments on diagnostic pools reveal a personalization imbalance in recommendation agents: relative to personalization signals alone, adding multimodal queries weakens preference following, even though the additional information about query requirements improves overall ranking performance. Further analysis links this decline in preference following to image interpretation, where agents can prioritize resemblance to reference images over evidence from user histories, and stronger commercial backbones alone fail to resolve this imbalance. This personalization imbalance highlights a central challenge for recommendation agents: improving ranking performance while preserving preference following when responding to multimodal user queries

title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench

title: When Predictive Fit Misleads: Selecting Marketing Mix Models Using Experimental RoAS Benchmarks
abstract: Marketing Mix Models (MMMs) are used to estimate channel-level Return on Ad Spend (RoAS) and guide marketing investment, yet competing specifications are usually compared on predictive-fit metrics such as out-of-sample R-squared, MAPE, or RMSE. We show that predictive fit can diverge from recovery of the causal quantities that drive marketing decisions. In simulations with known RoAS, the best-fitting specification is often not the one that recovers RoAS most accurately; replicated studies show that this disagreement is systematic and persists under media-spend collinearity, noise, and a misspecified carryover shape. Selecting specifications against experimental RoAS benchmarks, even imprecise ones, improves RoAS recovery relative to fit-based selection, and a real-world application with experimental benchmarks shows the same pattern. We propose an applied workflow: calibrate MMM specifications against estimand-aligned experimental benchmarks when they exist, and otherwise report RoAS sensitivity across plausible specifications rather than relying on a single best-fitting model.

title: Beyond Risk Cues: A Mechanism-Level Benchmark and Verifiable Debate for Scam Video Detection on the Web
abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.

title: GeoBiaset: A Counterfactual Benchmark for Demographic Bias in World-Level Geolocalization
abstract: World-level image geolocalization is an increasingly important task, yet the biases of current models remain poorly understood. Prior work has identified coarse dataset imbalances noting, for instance, that some cities are absent from training sets and that models tend to perform better in wealthier regions. However, no one has yet examined which visual cues drive these disparities. To do so, we introduce GeoBiaset, the first benchmark designed to measure how geolocalization models are influenced by the apparent race of a person inserted into the image foreground. The dataset consists of 9,541 images, pairing existing geotagged background images with counterfactual edits spanning seven races, holding the ground-truth coordinates fixed. Controlled masking experiments show that occlusion and background drift do not fully explain geolocalization degradation. Alongside the benchmark, we introduce the Person-Origin Perturbation Indicators (POPI), novel metrics that quantify model resilience to these demographic perturbations by measuring whether predictions are pulled toward the region associated with the inserted group. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art geolocalization and multimodal large language models reveals a 16-47% drop in continent-level performance when a subject from a demographically mismatched group is inserted. A landmark versus no-landmark analysis and gradient-weighted heatmaps show that models preferentially attend to geographic landmarks when present, but shift attention to facial features in their absence.

title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.

title: Intra-Architecture Source Attribution for Stable Diffusion: A New Task with Benchmark Dataset and Baseline
abstract: Designing systems that attribute a generated image to its source model has lately become a major area of AI research. Most existing datasets and systems related to image source attribution are targeted towards the detection of architectural signatures of the source models. Distinct from this, focusing on stable diffusion, we introduce a novel task, IntrAA-SD, Intra-Architecture source Attribution for Stable Diffusion, where the source models to be differentiated share the same architectural backbone and differ only due to fine-tuning. The proposed task aligns with the emergence of fine-tuned generators having the same architecture, like Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL, which are fine-tuned versions of Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL). We provide a first-of-its-kind $140$K-image benchmark dataset containing images generated from different fine-tunes of SDXL, along with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. We also provide a baseline framework for IntrAA-SD, which leverages a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts network. It uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture the image style and gate the MoE, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network. The fine-tuned models used, the prompting strategies considered, and the formation details employed in the novel dataset are elaborated. Our baseline intra-architecture source attribution method is evaluated in terms of attribution accuracy on our dataset, and ablation studies are also performed. Code and dataset is available at https://github.com/mallikagarg/IntrAA-SD.

title: WayPOP: A Panoramic Open-Set Panoptic Tracking Benchmark
abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.
